claims.text: High configurational disorder stabilizes a homogeneous bcc lattice in high-entropy alloy superconductors.
High configurational disorder enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Compositional disorder creates distributed vortex-pinning centers.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling and distributed vortex pinning make superconductivity more robust against external perturbations.
The proposed initial material is a single-phase, compositionally disordered high-entropy alloy with a bcc lattice.
The controlled comparison changes from a five-or-more-component near-equiatomic alloy to a binary or ternary alloy.
The lower-entropy baseline is to be matched to the high-entropy alloy in average electron count and bcc crystal structure.
Low-temperature resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements can identify superconducting transitions in these high-entropy alloys.
Pressure-dependent resistivity measurements can track Tc in a high-entropy alloy over a pressure range.
The high-entropy alloy will have a higher Tc than the matched lower-entropy baseline.
The high-entropy alloy's Tc will be less sensitive to pressure than that of the lower-entropy baseline.
The high-entropy alloy's superconducting transition will be less sensitive to magnetic-field variation than that of the lower-entropy baseline.
The high-entropy alloy will have a higher upper critical field than the matched lower-entropy baseline.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to conventional type-II superconductors with bcc lattices and electron–phonon-dominated pairing.
The mechanism may not apply to superconductors with unconventional pairing.
The mechanism may not apply to alloys with significant phase segregation.
Prior studies support a causal role for high configurational disorder in stabilizing superconductivity.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in Tc stability and Hc2 relative to the matched baseline would falsify the proposed disorder-governed enhancement.
